Now, the resolution of the hon. member (Mr. Smith) is quite contrary to the one proposed by my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux). The mover of the resolution wants the embargo retained; my hon. friend from Maisonneuve seeks to have it removed. The question is a very old one. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Maisonneuve that we have the right to remonstrate in regard to any question that effects us prejudicially, and that as British subjects it is our privilege to go and state our views before the government of the Old Country. But having stated them fully and accurately, I do not see what there is to be gained by our continuing to nag at the British Government. As I say, this is an old story. Several hon. gentlemen have given us dates of the embargoes. I remember a good many years ago when Lord Onslow was Minister of Agriculture in the British Government. I had discussed the matter with him. I happened to be in England soon after there was a change of government. Meeting Lord Onslow I said: " I see that C. B. has come in C. B. was the familiar designation of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman-" and I presume that the folk who have been agitating for the removal of the embargo will now have their way." He said:	" I bet you they
won't." Well, I did not take the bet, and it was well that I did not, for I should have lost. Some British politicians occasionally argue in favour of the abolition of the embargo, but the Department of Agriculture of the British Government -strongly supported by the landed interests of England-have been determined to keep it up, and they will continue to do so. But the embargo is no longer put upon the ground that there is disease in Canadian cattle. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) says that what he complains of is the libel which the embargo places upon our cattle. Well, he is mistaken, for if ever disease was attributed as a reason for the embargo that is no longer the case. The reason is entirely one of self-protection on the part of the British people. They admit freely that our cattle are free from disease. But it is argued that there is more than a possibility of disease being introduced from the United States through Canada and in that way affecting the cattle in the Mother Country. That is the sole ground on which they place the embargo. I read recently a very interesting article from the pen of Lord Crewe on this subject. He was formerly Colonial Secretary, and to-day, I think, he is leader of the Liberal Opposition in the British House of Lords. He has written a strong letter regarding the action of Lord Lee, President of the Board of Agriculture, who preceded the member that was defeated the other day, and he says that the agriculturists of England are standing behind Lord Lee in this matter, and will insist on this regulation being kept up. I am inclined to think that at bottom it was a protective measure; I have a suspicion that it was designed to protect the cattle raisers of England and Ireland. An hon. member says that he wants them to admit that. Well, did you ever know a man to admit a protective policy squarely as such? You sometimes adopt measures which some people describe as protective, but you hate to call them so yourself, and that is about the situation to-day in England. I thing that this measure is retained owing to their desire-a desire with which hon. gentlemen opposite should not, I think, find fault-to protect the cattle trade of England and Ireland. In recent days, however, as I have already stated, disease in Canada is no longer given as a reason for the embargo, and the British authorities make this absolutely clear. The letter of Lord Crewe, to which I have already referred, and the declarations of other authorities in England, emphatically state that the cattle of Canada are free from disease. This being the case, therefore, I do not see that there is any libel on Can-

ada. It is contended, however, that there is a danger of cattle disease being brought into England from the United States through Canada.

Has any
statement been made by the British House of Commons to the effect that the embargo is merely a measure of protection?

I do not suppose that the British Commons have made any such declaration; I should not expect it. But even if that is so, I think it is beyond dispute that the ground is no longer taken that the embargo is due to any disease in our cattle. That reason has been abandoned, and it is now useless to argue against the embargo on the ground that there is any objection to our cattle by reason of disease. The British Board of Agriculture admit that there is no disease in Canadian cattle; Lord Crewe and Lord Lee both admit the same thing; and all the literature on the subject is clear that the whole ground, good or bad, has nothing to do with any question of disease in our cattle.

As the hon. member is
a student of this subject, may I ask him to go further and state that Lord Beaver-brook's contention was not one in favour of the admission of Canadian cattle but in favour of cheap meat and cheap bread? That is the whole question.

I would rather not introduce Lord Beaverbrook into the matter; but I quite agree that if we feel aggrieved in this matter at all, it is our right as citizens and as a Parliament to remonstrate. Having remonstrated, and having the facts clearly placed before us, I think all will agree with me that is is rather undignified to keep nagging on the question all the time. It is a matter entirely for the British people, although we may have the right to think they are wrong. I think they are wrong in the matter, but since, after full deliberation the British Government and the British Parliament, the leaders of public opinion in Great- Britain-those who have a powerful influence, or practically speaking, the controlling influence in the British Parliament, in the House of Lords, in the House of Commons and in the various departments-have made up their minds, are we to be continually asking them to recede from their position? I have no objection to it being declared that the Canadian people think the embargo is a mistake, but I do not think the matter is one which we should

threaten and bluster and make a great fuss about, and make it appear that the British Government and the British Parliament are treating us in a very bad way. The matter is one which is entirely within their right. They have a right to be wrong if they want to, and I am quite willing to concede that to them.

If I believed that the removal of the embargo would discourage the finishing of cattle in Canada, or necessarily discourage us in establishing abattoirs, I would be disposed to vote for the resolution of my hon. friend because he probably knows more about the live stock industry than any other man in this House. But I have not heard anything to convince me that the removal of the embargo would interfere in the least with the finishing of beef cattle in Canada. I had hoped that when my hon. friend was dealing with the question he would have given us some information upon it because his knowledge is probably better than that of the majority of us. I would have liked to have heard him state what the effect of the embargo has been in the matter of encouraging people to finish cattle in Canada for the English market. If he could have told us the average price paid for Canadian cattle when they reached Liverpool or Scotland, compared with the price of the best Scotch finished beef, and if he could have satisfied us that the Canadian cattle being shipped across under present conditions would bring as high a price as the best Scotch finished animals, I would have said there is a great deal in his argument. But I do not think my hon. friend can give us figures showing anything of the kind. I am rather inclined to think that the price which we receive for our finished stock is not to be for one moment compared with the highest price paid for the stock finished in Scotland. I do not think my hon. friend will for one moment claim that the price paid for Canadian animals comes anyway near the price paid for the Scottish animals. Therefore, if I am right in my supposition, it shows the maintenance of the embargo is an absolute failure for the purpose for which my hon. friend wishes it maintained-it has not had the effect which he thinks it would have.
If that be so we must consider the case from some other standpoint. I would not for one moment wish to be associated with any interference with British legislators. My hon. friend's argument might be argument advanced in opposition to the resolu-

tion placed on the Order Paper by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) ; it is not argument in favour of the present resolution. If the present resolution means anything at all it amounts to an attempt to give advice to the British legislators * and I think that in England it will be looked upon as such. I think it will Be looked upon there as a bit of advice from this House recommending them to maintain the embargo. It seems to me that that is the only way in which it can be regarded. Therfore I fail to see anything whatever in such an argument.
Let me go back to the question of the finishing of cattle. I do not think that every part of the world is suited to the finishing of beef cattle. As a matter of fact I doubt very much if the cattle that we look upon in Canada as finished would be accepted in Liverpool as finished animals at all. I do not think they can for a moment be compared with the finished animals that the Scotchman turns out.
I am advised that a great many of the Irish feeders do not finish their cattle at all, and their finished cattle are very jnuch better than ours from Western Canada. I am advised that a very large proportion of the Irish feeders ship their cattle to Scotland for the Scotchmen to finish, because the Scotchman makes a specialty of finishing those animals which are sent from different parts of Great Britain. If that be so why not let him have a chance of finishing some of ours. We can turn out very good stock but I do not think we have ever got the habit-not even our best feeders-of finishing our cattle as they are finished there. I say that the Irishman, whom I am advised ships his cattle to Scotland to he finished, is in a very much better position to do that finishing than we are, especially those of us in the western country.
It is not the first time I have listened to lectures from my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) as to how we should farm in the West. I suggest to my hon. friend that it would he better to leave the western farmers to work out their own salvation rather than that advice should come from people who do not know what they are talking about. We out there know very much better how to overcome the difficulties in our way or what should be done to meet them, we are very much better informed about that country than is my hon. friend. With all due deference to him we know some of the difficulties we have had to encounter; and any man who has been identified with
feeding stock in the western country knows there are many difficulties in the way of finishing that stock as it should be finished for the British market. In time we may overcome those difficulties; but the solution will have to he worked out, it cannot he arrived at all at once. The present embargo is a great handicap to us in shipping cattle to Great Britain and so long as it continues in force that will continue to be the case. The western farmers feel very keenly that so long as that embargo remains they will be very seriously handicapped, and I submit that they know a great deal more about the situation there than my hon. friend from Ontario.

You have had it
for twenty-nine years.
That is true.
' I mean the embargo.

I thought it was our farming operations you were referring to. The embargo has been in force for some time and it may be in force for some time yet. So long as it is there it will be a barrier-not merely an embargo, but a barrier to our success at stock raising in so far as we depend upon the British market. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I have no other alternative than to vote against the resolution of my hon. friend. While I shall vote in that way I do not say that I would vote in favour of any resolution presented here asking for a removal of that embargo; that would require separate and very careful consideration. I certainly am opposed to any resolution such as the present one which to my mind is practically a bit of advice offered to the British Parliament that they should keep the embargo on and that we do not want it removed. With that I cannot agree.

The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat took, if I may say so, a somewhat peculiar position in the last few sentences which he uttered. He objects to the resolution proposed by the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith), on the ground that it is giving advice to the British Government and asking them to retain the embargo. He says, however, in regard to a resolution which would ask for the removal of the embargo, and which would certainly be a greater interference on our part than the present resolution, that he would give such a resolution some con-

sideration; that he would not be prepared to vote against that on the same ground as he would vote against the present one because it would meet his own views-he could not see in the other resolution the interference which he apparently sees in' the resolution now before the House. That, with all due respect to the fact that my hon. friend is a lawyer and supposed to argue questions and come to a right conclusion, strikes me as rather a peculiar attitude.
I would also say a word in regard to the attitude of the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), or, since this is a subject more especially concerning people who live in rural districts, the hon. member for Gaspe. Of course, on industrial questions we will refer to him as representing his other constituency. But on this question the hon. member for Gaspe has assumed a somewhat peculiar position also. I was surprised to hear him taking rather strong exception to some utterances by Lord Beaverbrook, especially because, if I read correctly the newspaper reports of what the noble lord said, I would certainly think that if he had a seat in this House he would vote for the resolution which stands in the name of the hon. member for Gaspe, as I can only infer from his utterances that Lord Beaverbrook is opposed to the embargo against Canadian cattle and wishes to have it removed. However, my hon. friend sees in the remarks, of Lord Beaverbrook a meddling in British affairs. If it is considered perfectly proper for an hon. gentlemen in this House to move a resolution which certainly can only be taken as a piece of gratuitous advice to the British authorities, I would think that a man who has a seat in the British Parliament might at least be allowed to express his opinions on British policy, and that, I believe, is all that Lord Beaverbrook has done.
Now, Sir, the hon. member for Gaspe has said that he does not want to be taken as interfering in British affairs or giving advice to the Old Country as to how they should regulate their policy in regard to the importation of cattle. He has expressed a belief, as have other hon. gentlemen, that this attitude on the part of the British Government in placing an embargo on cattle from Canada and the United States and other countries is not due, so far as Canada is concerned at least, to any belief on their part that our cattle are diseased. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was very emphatic in expressing that view, in which I

entirely concur. If that is true, if we are convinced that the British people do not entertain the thought that our cattle are diseased, then we must look for another reason for the embargo, and that reason strikes me as being purely and simply an attempt to protect their cattle industry, that is all it amounts to. Then, if my hon. friend from Gaspe does not want to appear as interfering or giving advice to Great Britain in the matter of her embargo policy, why does not his resolution state exactly what he does want? Really what he wants to get from the British Government is a statement, duly signed, sealed and witnessed, I suppose, to the effect that they do not believe our cattle are diseased. If that is the case, then his resolution should state that, and that alone. Great Britain has a right to arrange her fiscal policy to suit herself, just as we have a similar right.
This debate, of course, has given the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) an opportunity to talk free trade again. I was expecting the hon. gentleman would get up, and I thought: What a wonderful opportunity he will have of-if I may use a common expression-lambasting the British Government for its protective policy in this instance. The hon. gentleman, however, had very little to say in condemnation of the British attitude. Still he must get off his free trade speech, and as he did not desire to say very much about the British policy, he took it out on Canada and gave us advice on what we should do in the way of developing more trade between the two countries.

May I put a
question to my hon. friend just with a view of elucidating this matter fully? Does not his case against Great Britain as to this embargo being a purely protective measure not fall down, somewhat at least, in view of the consideration that Great Britain imports any amount of dead meat without duty?

I do not think it does, because Great Britain evidently believes that in keeping on this embargo she is protecting her own livestock industry. My hon. friend will not say that that embargo is being continued in order to protect British stock men from diseased cattle? Then what is the object if it is not to protect them in the raising of livestock? Undoubtedly the embargo is purely a protective measure on their part, and I think that every hon. member recognizes it as such. If Great Britain placed a duty of

$100 per head on imported Canadian cattle, no person here would raise any question at all; we would recognize her right to do so. But an import duty of $100 a head would not be any more prohibitive against our cattle than thg present embargo; they would both serve exactly the same purpose, which is absolutely one of protection.
I gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for South Ontario, who is a very experienced stock man and one to whom we always listen with interest and profit, that it would be in the best interests of Canadian livestock men to finish their product here rather than ship it to England partly finished, as they would do if the embargo was taken oif. In that I entirely agree with him. I am not inclined to altogether agree with him that the best place for abattoirs would be in Halifax, because if the argument holds good that in shipping the live animal from Halifax we would be shipping a lot of waste material, it would also apply in shipping stock, we will say, from Ontario to Halifax, and so the abattoirs might be better placed nearer the point where the animals are being finished. I do think, especially in view of action which the United States may take, that the Government would be well advised in establishing abattoirs in various parts of the country in order to encourage those in the livestock industry to finish their animals and ship them in the form of meat rather than on the hoof.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, may I add this? It is unfair to expect our livestock men to compete on even terms with the stock raisers of the Argentine or of the Southern States, for instance, Texas. There again I want to say-and this I pass on for the special benefit of the hon. member for Red Deer-that the Government should, if anything, raise the duty on live animals coming-into this country. It is unfair to ask our farmers and stock raisers with the disadvantages of our climate, to compete on even terms with Southern States like Texas or with South American countries like the Argentine, where they have no winter conditions to contend with. This is something, it seems to me, which even my hon. friend from Red Deer, ardent free trader as he is, might do well to consider when he is preaching his free trade doctrine in this House. - The hon. gentleman loses sight entirely of the climatic conditions we have to contend with when he is talking free trade whether in regard to cattle or anything else. He knows perfectly well that the farmers of this country have thousands of dollars invested in barns and stables to take care of their stock, and that they must be put to very great expense in fitting their cattle for the market. In that respect their competitors in Argentina and Texas have a very great advantage over them. These are things which should be considered in this connection.
Another thing which the Government might well consider-and I advanced this view in the House a year or two ago-is the desirability of giving Canadian flour shipped from Canadian ports to the markets of Europe a preference over wheat in the matter of ocean rates, thus inducing the milling of more wheat in this country and making available to Canadian farmers the by-products of wheat which they must have if they are to compete with those parts of the United States and those other countries which are more fortunate than we are as respects climatic conditions. All these things, it seems to me, are worthy of consideration in connection with this matter. But I most strongly deprecate this House undertaking, in connection with this resolution or with any other resolution, to tell Great Britain what she should do in handling her own affairs. Let Great Britain handle her affairs as she deems best, and we can maintain the right to do the same for ourselves. They have never undertaken to advise us in matters of legislation; very often this House has undertaken to advise Great Britain, a procedure which, I think, is not only undignified, but borders very closely on the impertinent.

- (Mackenzie):	Mr. Speaker, I wish to make just a few observations on this resolution, which I consider to be a very important one. Should the resolution carry, it will be an admission on our part, as I read it, that our Canadian cattle are diseased. It says:
That, in the opinion of this House, it would not be in the interests of Canada should the Government of Great Britain remove the embargo upon cattle going into the United Kingdom.
It is well known that the reason why our cattle are not admitted free into Great Britain is because of the discovery of disease in them some years ago. It has been suggested that the embargo is a measure of protection on behalf of the British stock raiser. I know for a fact that Scottish stock feeders want to be able to purchase our Canadian stocker:	several of
them have told me that our cattle are thi

best and the healthiest that they can buy. The same applies to the English farmer. But the protection is a protection for Ireland, for the Irish farmer, and, I think, Mr. Speaker, we will all agree that Ireland needs a little protection.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. White) has voiced the sentiments of western stock men to the effect that if something is not done to stabilize the stock industry, especially in the West, the stock-raisers will practically have to go out of business. Then, I think the Government should make some inquiries with regard to the building of abattoirs. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), in advancing the argument that our stock should be finished at home advocated the use of smaller farms and the employment of more men on the land. I just want to say in passing that if that principle were adapted, the revenue from an income tax point would be considerably decreased. In Saskatchewan the farmers paid $340,000 by way of income tax-I am giving the round figures and speaking partly from memory, so that I am subject to correction. think, therefore, that it would be wise, even for the sake of obtaining the benefit which would result from finishing our live stock on the farms, to encourage small holdings.
