If practicable, we should ask Great Brtiain to remove the embargo, and should the Government consider it advisable to do this, I suggest that they should say to the British Government at the same time: If you will remove the embargo on our Canadian cattle, we will take off all the duties against British manufactured goods.

Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity of speaking on this question a good-many times, and though I cannot profess to be quite up to date on the subject I think I may be justified in placing a few facts before the House in reference to the conditions as they existed a few years ago.
Five years after the embargo was placed upon our Canadian cattle, there was still a strong agitation to have the embargo removed. At that time I asked the Customs Department to furnish me with a statement of the number of cattle shipped during the five years prior to the placing of the embargo and the five years following the placing of the embargo. I am sorry to say that I have not these figures before me, though I kept them for many years; probably they are still among my treasures. But it may be broadly stated that prior to the placing of the embargo an immense export trade in live cattle had been carried on from Ontario to the United Kingdom and the cattle were bringing at that time a very high price. If my memory serves me correctly, the average price obtained for Canadian cattle at the time the embargo went on was about $95 per head. As we were sending hundreds of thousands of cattle into the British market, that meant many millions of dollars for the province of Ontario alone. Immediately after the embargo was imposed, the number of cattle exported diminished very rapidly, and the price decreased just as rapidly as the number of cattle exported diminished, thus showing conclusively, to my mind, that we lost a very valuable market by an act which I always considered to be a great injustice to the Dominion. It is quite true, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. (Mr. Fielding) said, that an effort was made lately to show that the embargo was not imposed on account of disease [DOT] tut the fact

is that the embargo was imposed in the first place on account of disease and no other disease than pleuro-pneumonia. The diseases which the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) mentioned were not in the category at all. While Canadian cattle were free from disease, there was a possibility that United States cattle were not; I believe they were not entirely free, and that, perhaps, there came across our borders into Canada a few cattle that were affected with disease. I believe, if anybody will go to the customs and ask for the figures, he will find that they prove that, after the passing of the embargo, the number of cattle exported fell off very rapidly and the price fell just as rapidly, so that we lost both ways.
The hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith) is one of the highest authorities on livestock matters, and I feel like a very humble member beside him in debating any of these questions pertaining to cattle. It is only because, in years gone by, I have made a considerable study of this question that I venture to make these few remarks. Taking it for granted that the best proposition is to send the finished cattle from Canada, that is, that they should be fed on our own grain and absolutely matured in Canada before they go to the British market, I want to point this out-and I do not think it has been mentioned so far in the debate-[DOT] that cattle travelling under sea conditions, herded and fed and watered as they are, are a good deal like men or women making the same voyage; they arrive in a condition, not fit to kill. I think the hon. member will realize the truth of that. I have crossed the Atlantic many times; I know what seasickness means, and I am told that cattle are just as much subject to seasickness as human beings. Therefore, when these cattle arrive at Liverpool and other markets, they are not in shape to kill; they have not been fed or watered or housed properly, and as a result they have lost a lot of flesh and the flesh that remains is not in a good condition. Anyone can understand that when an animal has been affected by seasickness for ten days or two weeks, it is not in a condition to kill, and in justice to the British people, they should not be fed on the flesh of cattle that have been killed in a seasick condition. Yet the regulations say that those animals must be slaughtered within ten days after arrival. The proposition on the face of it is not a good one.
It is said that Lord Beaverbrook is conducting a Canadian campaign, but I am not sure that he has said that it is a Canadian
campaign he is conducting. I am sorry this has become a political issue in the Old Country; I hope it will not become a political issue in Canada, and perhaps the best course for us to pursue at the present time is to say very little about the matter either one way or the other. I have never known my hon. friend (Mr. Smith) to go wrong on agricultural matters; but, perhaps, he is not going to divide the House on this question and I shall not have to oppose him at present. The cattle question in Canada is to my mind one amongst a number of burning questions, and in Ontario with the Minister of Agriculture of that province going overseas in order to push the matter, it has become a more live question than usual. Whether that gentleman has any mandate from Ontario to go and push that question, I am not so clear. I think, perhaps, on the whole, as we have on the Order Paper these two resolutions, pro and con, the better idea would be to withdraw them both and let the debate go for what it is worth. For myself, I believe an injustice is being done to Canada; that it ought to be removed and that we should not be told our cattle are diseased. To the hon. member for South Ontario, I would say that it is not necessary for us to take advantage of the removal of the embargo, if it is not to our interest to do so, but we would have the privilege of taking advantage of it if there is anything to be gained.
I cannot refrain from pointing this out to my good friend the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) because, although he made some remarks on the cattle question, he strayed a little afield, when he said that we could never expect in this country to have the trade that we should have unless we brought back full ships as well as sent out full ships. I think that was the idea the hon. gentleman had. You may build all the ships in the world; but when you bring in more than half the goods that come into Canada, by rail, and not by ships,-and that is a policy which my hon. friend is pushing for all he is worth, namely, to bring in goods from the United States by rail- you will never have full ships crossing the Atlantic. I would support my hon. friend if he said that we should buy more British goods than American; then he would be talking; but, at present, goods are being brought in by a short rail route from the United States, much to the detriment of our railways that need the traffic, as can be seen by looking at the railway Estimates, instead of being brought in by ships to

Halifax, St. John, Quebec, and being loaded on our railways, thus furnishing a trade route throughout the whole country. Out of about i$l,500,000,000 worth of goods that we have brought into Canada, nearly $1,000,000,000 have come from the United States, and, I believe, almost entirely by rail. So I say to the hon. member for Red Deer: You cannot fill ships on that basis The difficulty is not that we are not buying enough goods; we are at the present time buying more than we are selling, but we are buying them in the wrong quarter.

May I remove
a misapprehension my hon. friend seems to be under? I never had the least idea of taking goods from or bringing goods to the United States in ships. It is the British trade to which I was referring.

My hon. friend said
that the reason why Canada did not have sufficient trade was because we were not buying enough, and we were not filling our ships because we did not bring in sufficient across the water. I am pointing out that we are buying too many goods, but in the wrong quarter, the United States, when we should be buying them from the Mother Country. If we did that, we would fill our ships; we would furnish transportation for our railways, and our cattle going to and fro would be filling those ships and the railway cars with the desired freight. I think my hon. friend will see that his policy of buying more goods is not what we need.
Would not an increase in the British preference cause us to buy more from Great Britain and less from the United States? That is what my hon. friend had in mind.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont) :
speechtext:
I just want to say a few words in this debate. While I have the greatest respect for my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Smith), whom I know to be a man who has been interested in the live stock industry for years, and who has done very much to improve the live stock business in the province of Ontario, I must differ from him on the resolution which he has submitted to the House this afternoon. The reason given, and it was given in this debate this afternoon, for the placing of an embargo upon our cattle, was that possibly disease might be brought into the

herds of the Old Land from Canada. I do not think there is any country in the world that has been so free from these diseases as Canada. The disease particularly mentioned in connection with this embargo is pleuro-pneumonia. We are told that there has been no case of pleuropneumonia in this country since 1886, and that the cases at that time were confined to a quarantine station. The disease did not get beyond the bounds of that station, and the animals were cremated, so there was no danger of a spread of infection from that source. It has also been stated that British cattle breeders fear that the foot and mouth disease might be introduced into Great Britain by our cattle, but there has been no outbreak of foot and mouth disease in this country since 1884, and the cases then were confined to a quarantine station; they never got beyond that. Very strict regulations were put in force by the Federal Department of Agriculture when live stock was being shipped from this country to the Old Land. Inspectors were stationed at all shipping points, and all the cattle for export had to undergo a very severe examination. Those regulations are ready to be put into force again should that trade be revived. Just to show that our Federal Department has the situation fully in hand, I would remind the House that in the last outbreak of foot and mouth disease across the line, which affected a great area, 23 states, I think, of the American Union, and cost the Americans hundreds of thousands of dollars, the quarantine regulations put into force by our department at that time prevented the disease spreading to the herds in this country. It was a very severe test that the Federal Department was put to at that time, and the result proves conclusively, I think, that there is no danger of disease from that source, because those regulations are still in force and should our cattle trade with the Old Land be revived the Federal Department could take the same measures to prevent the spread of infection from our herds to the Old Land.
My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has given a few figures on the export trade from Canada to Great Britain before the embargo was placed on our live cattle. That trade, of course, fell off, but during the last few years since the United States has been admitting our cattle free, quite a large trade has developed across the line in live cattle. Since 1914 there have been, in round figures,
200,000 cattle per year sent across the line; in some years, a few more, and in others perhaps less. Valuing these at $100 per head, the trade would amount to about $20,000,000 per year, a very valuable trade indeed.
It has been argued in this debate that it would be better for Canada to finish her store cattle at home, to feed them here, and place them on the British market in a finished condition. Canada cannot do that at the present time. On account of our wide areas, our rather extensive pasture areas, our scarcity of labour, Canada can rear and produce far more cattle than she can finish. Our present stage of development is better fitted for rearing and producing a far greater number of cattle than we can finish. On the other hand, the British farmer, who carries on operations on a far more intensive scale than we do, is in a better position to take these cattle and finish them. He will stable them, feed them high, and finish them in a short time, and have a quick turnover. He can finish more than one group in one year, whereas the Canadian farmer would require two, three or four years in order to produce and rear the cattle that he has to sell. There is no question, however, that a great number of cattle are being finished in our country, and placed on the markets of the world in a finished condition, and undoubtedly in the future the number will be larger. But under present conditions, where we have large areas of pasture, and a scarcity of labour, the Canadian farmer can produce and rear far more cattle than he can finish, and it would be of great advantage to him as well as to the British farmer to have the embargo removed, so that he could produce and rear a large number of store cattle, to be shipped ovter to Great Britain and finished there.
I do not at all underestimate the value of the finishing of our cattle here and placing them upon any market in that condition. That, of course, is desirable, and it is an end towards which we are working. But at the present time we have a large surplus of store cattle, and if we cannot get them out of the country we shall suffer a very great loss. I have already spoken in regard to the trade that has developed between Canada and the United' States in this regard. We have heard something in the last few days concerning the Fordney Bill. Now, should this Bill or any other of a similar character be carried into effect and our trade with the



United States be cut off, there would be an immense glut of store cattle on the Canadian market', and if the British embargo were removed we should immediately have an outlet for this produce to take the place of the American market.
There is another phase of this question upon which I should like to touch. I understand, although I am not certain on this point, that the embargo applies not only to our cattle but to our sheep as well. Canada, of course, is not a great sheep-producing country, nor, on the other hand, is she a great mutton-consuming nation, and at certain seasons of the year there is a considerable glut of mutton on the Canadian market. If the embargo were removed an outlet would be provided for our live sheep and it would ensure us against these gluts that occasionally occur in this country.
There is another feature of this question which is sometimes overlooked. The British herds and flocks have been a source from which Canadian breeders have imported a great deal of stock for the improvement of their own cattle and sheep. If the embargo were removed and our live cattle were allowed to enter Great Britain free, there is no doubt whatever that the return trade that would result of pure-bred stock from the Old Land would improve our herds, particularly in regard to bulls, in which respect our herds in this country are lamentably deficient. Just in this connection I may say that since this trade has developed with the United States there have been coming into this country particularly into the Canadian West a considerable number of pure-bred bulls. If the embargo were removed I feel sure that the British breeders would compete and share in that trade, and the result would be a very valuable improvement in the herds and flocks of the livestock men of this country.
Do English animals come into Canada free of duty?

I think the pure-bred animals come free of duty. The Old Country has been a very fertile source of purebred stock for Canadian breeders, and there is no question that our herds have been greatly improved by importations from their herds. We must admit that in many cases they are ahead of us in this business, and we should cultivate this return trade to as great an extent as possible. I should be sorry indeed to see the resolution proposed by my hon. friend from

South Ontario (Mr. Smith) carried in this House.

speakeroldname: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Victoria City, B. C.) :
speechtext:
In rising to say a few words on this resolution I desire at the outset to pay a tribute to the mover for the excellent service he has rendered the livestock interests of Canada during his years of experience as a breeder and importer in the province of Ontario. He is one of our oldest, most respected, and most capable breeders of purebred stock, being known all the way from the Atlantic to the Pacific. He has been not only a successful exhibitor at many of our fairs, but has filled the important position of judge on many an occasion on both sides of the line. However, I feel that on this occasion I cannot quite agree with him on this embargo question. In the first place, when the embargo was imposed, the argument was advanced that Canadian cattle were affected with contagious disease,-at that time pleuropneumonia. The adoption of this resolution might convey the impression that we are perfectly satisfied and have been satisfied for thirty years, with this embargo, whereas, as a matter of fact, ever since the embargo was imposed the Government have from time to time been making regular efforts to have it removed.
The embargo was put on about thirty years ago on the assumption that pleuropneumonia had appeared in a shipment of cattle from Canada to the Old Country. I very well remember the occasion. I was then a student of veterinary science in Toronto and this matter was discussed at college on many occasions, and I remember distinctly that many veterinarians of Great Britain strongly protested against the diagnosis that was made by the official veterinary authorities on that occasion. It is about thirty-four years or more now since we last had a case of pleuro-pneu-monia in Canada, and as the previous speaker informed the House, it occurred in a shipment sent over here. That shipment remained in quarantine for the regular period and the animals were destroyed and the premises disinfected. It is about thirty-six years since there was a case of foot-and-mouth disease in Canada, which occurred in exactly the same way. It also was stopped in quarantine and it got no further. But there is every proof that our cattle are free from disease. As you know, we have the privilege of shipping cattle to Great Britain for salughter at the port of entry, and during the intervening period since the imposition of the

embargo we have slaughtered no fewer than three million head of Canadian cattle on the British side, under British inspection, and not one single case of pleuropneumonia has been discovered.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. speaker, ever since the embargo was imposed our Governments have been making efforts to secure its removal, and in 1917 the then Prime Minister, (Sir Robert Borden) received a distinct promise from the Minister of Agriculture of Great Britain, that the embargo would be removed. Shortly after that two delegates were sent from Canada to Great Britain to instruct the people regarding the health of Canadian cattle and also to represent the unfairness of imposing this embargo on the ground of disease in our cattle. They did this work entirely with the approval of the Minister of Agriculture of Great Britain and clearly through official channels. They interviewed many organizations of livestock breeders, labour organizations, etc., and also took up the matter with the press of the country. They rendered a very excellent service but one that had no effect. It is now rather regrettable that this matter has assumed a political aspect and that certain men are trying to make political capital out of the embargo situation. Lord Lee clearly stated a short time ago that if he undertook to remove the embargo, or had any business with the Government of Canada with reference to the subject, it would be through the proper channel, the Federal Department of Agriculture. It is unfortunate, therefore, that this matter has been taken up in the way that it has by some of the representatives from this side, and also by some of the press, with the result, I think, that the work has been hindered to a very great extent in as much as people have been very much irritated and they have misinterpreted the intentions of those who have been carrying on that campaign.
Now with regard to our markets, is the removal of this embargo going to help the cattle industry of Canada? I may say that at the present time we cannot possibly consume the number of beef cattle produced in this country at home. The result is that we have to look for an export market. We have been shipping these cattle to the United States, but there are rumors of tariff changes over there that will prevent our cattle from going into that market if those changes are approved. I want to say here that on the fourteenth of January I had the pleasure of addressing the American National Live Stock Association
46i
assembled at El Paso, Texas. This Association represents all the range cattle breeders of the United States extending from Texas to California, from California north to Washington, and East as far as the Dakotas. Those men were unanimously in favour of imposing duties on Canadian and Mexican cattle coming into the United States, so that if that market is removed we are going to have a little difficulty- in the beginning at least-in disposing of our surplus products. If we could place those cattle on the British market we could do so to great advantage, and a nice outlet would be provided for our cattle during the period in which we are getting our farmers to become feeders of livestock.
I quite admit that it would be much more beneficial, from an economic standpoint, to finish off the cattle in this country than to ship' over our chilled beef to Great Britain. Let us see for a moment what kind of luck we would have in carrying on work of that kind? I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who stated that the Government should have taken up an active policy immediately after the close of the war to get our meat on the British market in competition with the Argentine and Australia. Perhaps you will remember, Mr. Speaker, that at that time, immediately after the conclusion of the war, owing to the lack of shipping, a large number of animals had accumulated in the Argentine and also in Australia; so that at that particular period the Argentine was placing chilled beef on the British market at from eleven to fourteen cents a pound, while the Canadians were asking twenty-five cents for their article. The shipping of chilled beef in competition with the Argentine and Australia would not at the present time, I am afraid, be a very profitable work to undertake. In the first place you will perhaps be astounded, Mr. Speaker, to know that of the million cattle passing annually through our inspection abattoirs less than ten per cent are fitted for export to the British Islands in competition with the beef from the two countries I have mentioned, on account of their small size, their poor quality, and their . lack of finish.
The Government has long recognized that situation and we -are making every effort to induce the farmers to feed and finish their cattle. We have introduced what is known as "A carlot and smaller group policy" at our various fat stock shows. We are giving special prizes for finished animals in carlots and in smaller

groups, and we have had very excellent results. Last year at Brandon Fat Stock Show there were some three hundred cattle on exhibition and a very excellent quality of cattle they were. At some other shows we have also had good results. We also may assist in the establishment of a large fat stock show in the city of Toronto along the lines of the big International Show held in Chicago. The International Show at Chicago brings together cattle breeders and finishers from all over the continent, and from both sides of the International boundary line, so that it has done a very great deal in stimulating the finishing of beef cattle. We hope that the Toronto show when it gets started, probably next winter, will have similar effects in stimulating the finishing of Canadian cattle.
But what are we going to do with our cattle in the meantime? If the United States imposes a duty we cannot ship them there; we must have some other outlet. Let me point out that what is a finished steer on the western ranges of Canada is just about ready to go into the hands of Scotch or English feeders to be finished to suit the taste of the British market. Over there they like very much fatter beef than we use on this side, so that when these cattle have been fed on the ranges of Alberta, or wherever they are fed out in the West, they can then be shipped profitably to Great Britain and sold to the feeders there to finish.
To give you an idea of what cattle are selling for in Great Britain at the present time-and this will perhaps explain the enquiry of some person who wondered how the labour men were interested in the shipment of cattle to Great Britain-let me say that at a recent sale that took place there beef steers brought $358, beef heifers $241, calves $94 and spring dairy cows $448 per head, showing that there would be a most excellent profit in shipping cattle to the Old Country from Canada.
Will my hon. friend give the comparable prices for Canadian cattle?

Finished beef steers for May delivery are quoted now in Western Canada, I understand, at about ten and a half to eleven cents per pound. Heifers would run about two cents per pound less than that. Fall calves would sell for $25 or $35, and dairy cows would run from $125 to $175 or $200 acording to quality.
There is another explanation for the very great difference in the prices paid for fresh killed beef. The Britisher, the man
min i
who has money, the middle class man, and all others, have a very keen appetite for fresh killed beef, and in that they show rather better taste, I think, than do Canadians. The prices run almost twice as much for fresh killed beef as can be obtained for chilled beef or frozen beef from overseas. So that by sending our beef cattle over there, we would not only be securing a good market for our output, but would also be catering to the tastes of the British consumer.
With regard to the objections raised by the Imperial Government to the shipment of cattle to Britain, let me say that one of their first arguments has been the possibility of getting disease from Canadian cattle. I want to say here as a veterinarian, and one who has kept in close touch with the handling of animal contagious diseases all over the world, that we are in a better shape in Canada to-day than almost any other country in the world. We have a Health of Animals Branch that is made up of men fully qualified for the work, men who not only have to be graduates of a well recognized veterinary institution, but must, in addition to that, pass a special examination before they are permitted to undertake this important work. The proof of what I am saying is the past history of contagious disease in Canada. You will remember that during recent years there have been several very serious outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease in the United States-a most infectious disease and very easily carried-and that our veterinarians here were successful in protecting us with a boundary line four thousand miles long, and not one single case of foot-and-mouth disease occurred in the Dominion during that time. This is a clear-cut answer to the claim of the British Government that disease may get in from the United States. In addition to that we have had on the western plains a disease known as dourine amongst horses, a disease that has existed there for a number of years. Not only were we able to clean that up entirely but our pathologist, Dr. Watson, who is at the head of our Pathological staff in the Health of Animals Branch, made a vaccine by which" he was able to easily diagnose the disease and to use the most up-to-date methods in cleaning it up. Then again the record of our Health of Animals Branch recently made in the dipping of 120,000 head of cattle in the province of Alberta for cattle mange to clean up the disease was successful to such an extent that we were able to raise

the blanket quarantine existing over an area of more than 2,600 square miles. I think that was one of the finest performances ever accomplished by any group of veterinarians anywhere in the world.
Now, touching again on this particular point of cattle coming in from the United States. I think there would be no difficulty whatever in guarding British herds against contamination by animals from that country. It would be no trouble to permanently mark those cattle on entry so as to prevent any of them being shipped to England by taking advantage of any arrangement that might be made between Canada and Great Britain for the shipment of our cattle over there.
I feel that perhaps we have no right to make suggestions to Great Britain about her domestic affairs, but, on the other hand, I feel that they should come out in the open and remove the stigma that has been placed on Canadian cattle. This stigma has done us considerable damage. When some of our cattle shippers attempted to send cattle over to the Continent immediately after the war, I understand, one country rejected Canadian cattle because of the fact that they were refused entry into Great Britain ostensibly on account of cattle disease being prevalent in Canada. That is one of the impressions that get abroad as a result of this embargo. Let me point out further that a year and a half ago we were asked to get a special permit from Great Britain to send a shipment of pure bred Holstein cattle to British Holstein breeders, but we were not successful, although only a few years before that a shipment of pure-bred Holsteins brought in by special license from Holland. Yet in Holland foot-and-mouth disease prevails most of the time.
We are importing from Great Britain pure-bred cattle under certain restrictive regulations that have placed us absolutely on the safe side; in other words, we have never had any disease as a result of those importations, although foot-and-mouth disease prevails in England from time to time. As I said a moment ago, we have not had a case here for over thirty-six years. So arguing from these premises, I submit it would be safer for Great Britain to import cattle from this country than it would be for us to import their cattle, although, as I have shown, we have been importing British pure-bred stock for several years so successfully that we have had no disease as a result.
I have been very pleased to notice the great interest that has been taken in this very important matter, and I think that the mover of the resolution has also been gratified, and in taking my seat I would ask him to be kind enough to favourably consider its withdrawal.

Mr. Speaker, after the many very excellent addresses that we have listened to this afternoon on this subject and one which is of so much importance to our stock breeders and cattlemen I think our labours of the afternoon would be abortive if the results were of a negative nature. In my judgment it is the opinion of the majority of those who have taken part in this debate that there is a grievance, and that some appeal should be made with a view to its removal. I am sorry that I was not present until the mover of this resolution (Mr. Smith) had got about half way through his speech, and I must say that, not being an expert in this business such as he is, I raise objection to the request embodied in his resolution with a certain amount of fear and trembling.
It is true, as has been emphasized by hon. members this afternoon, that Great Britain has claimed a reason for an embargo being placed on our cattle. And from my experience and knowledge of the live stock business extending over a period almost as long as that of the previous speaker (Mr. Tolmie), who said this country has been free from both tubercular and foot and mouth disease for over thirty-six years, I think it is really desirable that something should be done to remove the stigma placed on our cattle by Great Britain. Therefore without delaying the House any longer, I would propose that the following amendment be made to the resolution:
That all the words after the word "House" In the resolution be struck out, and the following inserted in lieu thereof: "the Government of Canada should make a strong protest against the reasons assigned by the British Gov-vernment that Canadian cattle are diseased as an excuse for placing an embargo on Canadian live cattle going into the United Kingdom."
I think that this amendment will embody the concensus of opinion as expressed by hon. members this afternoon, and will accomplish something more than would be possible by merely allowing the matter to rest where it is at the moment and withdraw the resolution. I have much pleasure therefore in moving this amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only

been able to follow the speech of the mover of the resolution (Mr. Smith) and the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) who sat down a few moments ago. The amendment moved by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) would seem to imply that such a protest had not been made. Surely he is aware that the history of the last thirty years is the history of protests made not only by the government in office when the embargo was first imposed, but made	almost	yearly sinceby	every	successive government.
The Government that was in office from 1896 to 1911 took, so far as I am aware, precisely the same position as regards this embargo as the Government that is in power to-day. The record, for example, of the 1917 conference on this subject is a record of about as definite and insistent a protest as any Government is capable of making on the very grounds stated in the amendment. I am utterly unable to understand what can be the object of an amendment urging a protest when protest has been the policy of Canada for thirty years and every measure that the successive officers of the Department of Agriculture and the numbers of successive governments could devise has been resorted to to push that process to the effective limit. If any hon. member who thinks oi supporting the amendment can make a suggestion as to what further can be done in the way of pressing or implementing the protest, then an amendment embodying that suggestion will be of value for the consideration of the House. I do not know what more could be done; it is on the ground of the implication embodied in the British policy that our protest has all along been lodged and is lodged to-day. It is on that ground that strong and determined action was taken at the conference to which I refer, and by reason of that ground the British Minister of Agriculture at that time was good enough to say that, at some date which I am sorry he did not specify-* I believe that, in rather indefinite language, he fixed it as the termination of the war-the Government would see that this embargo was removed. The case of Canada to-day rests most strongly upon that promise, and, basing our claim on that promise and on the wrong done to this country by the implication, the Government of to-day is losing no time and sparing no effort to have the embargo removed.
Now, there is a way by which these negotiations or the continuance of this protest

can be carried on. There is a proper way, consistent with the full exercise of authority of the British Government and Parliament within their own domain and consistent with the principle that there shall be no interference from outside with the exerciseing of that authority. I do not think that even for the sake of bringing about the removal of the embargo we would be justified in stepping beyond that method. We have sought through the appropriate channels, through the channels constitutionally established, to bring home to the British Government the wrong done by the implication embodied in the embargo, and nothing has been left undone in that regard. But I do not think it is a proper function of this country or of authorities within this country to launch or initiate among the British people a propaganda against the course taken by the British Government. From that action we have refrained, but we have refrained from nothing in the way of making known the facts as to Canadian cattle in order that the British people may understand that there is no justification in fact for the implication. We have not, however, gone the length of endeavouring to instigate the British people against their own Administration, of endeavouring to launch a propaganda amongst the people against the conduct of their Government. I know that were similar action taken by British authorities against the conduct of this Government, no matter how unpopular the conduct of this Government might be, such action would be resented here. Nor do I understand how we could ever in future resent corresponding action on their part if we made ourselves guilty of initiating the process. I say, therefore, that through the proper channels, and by the proper methods, we will not cease to bring home to the British Government our conviction that if they intend to protect the breeder of stock in England, or protect whatever they like to protect, they should not do so in such a manner as to carry a false implication against the livestock of Canada.
I rose, however, only to suggest to the mover of the amendment-for I had no intimation that any amendment was intended-that it is scarcely fair to ask the House to lodge a protest that is already lodged, and that it is hardly going to put this House in a position of very great dignity as respects the British Government to pass a motion now asking that we do

that which the British Government knows we have never ceased to do for thirty years.

I am sorry that I have not been able to follow the discussion of this resolution, but after hearing my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, I feel impelled to say a word or two as to why I am in favour of the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow).
The Prime Minister states that this Government has lodged protests on many occasions; that it has kept on lodging protests against that embargo. Well, what is the objection to the Parliament of Canada stating emphatically by way of resolution that we support the Government in the lodging of that protest?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No objection.
There is no objection, then, to my hon. friend's amendment. If it is the wish of members on both sides of the House, why not incorporate it in the form of resolution as my hon. friend suggests?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The amendment does not say that. If the amendment was drawn that way, there would be no objection to it.

Well, it might be
worded as I suggest. I must express my concurrence in the view that we should not interfere with the policies of Britain. I admit quite freely that we would resent any such interference on the part of Britain with our own policies. But there is another consideration in regard to this embargo. Britain is at liberty to prohibit the entrance of our cattle into her country, but what I strongly object to is the reason given for that prohibition. If such a reason were given for similar action by any foreign country we would resent it, and we resent 'it when it comes from Britain, and the fact that it is done by Britain is no reason why we should not say so in this Canadian Parliament. Let them place an embargo on our Canadian cattle if they like, but we resent the reasons they are giving. Our cattle are not diseased, and it is a slander against one of the main articles of Canadian production to assign that reason for any embargo.
Mr. PETER ' McGIBBON (Muskoka) (rising).
I would just like to reply briefly to-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman (Mr. Pedlow) would certainly be out of order in replying to the remarks of the Prime Minister unless he did so with the unanimous consent of the House. The hon. member who moves a substantive motion has the right to reply, but the amendment is not a substantive motion; therefore, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) has not that right unless it is given to him by unanimous consent of the House. Do I understand that the hon. member from Muskoka desires to say a word?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to support the view expressed here this afternoon, that Canada, who guards so jealously her own rights and privileges, should refrain from interfering with similar rights and privileges enjoyed by the Mother Country. I recognize that there has been a reflection upon Canada in the charge that her cattle have been diseased.
When the late Sir Charles Tupper was acting as High Commissioner in England, this question first came up. He engaged some of the best veterinary surgeons in England, and on several occasions he had Canadian cattle slaughtered when they arrived in that country and their lungs and other organs examined for tuberculosis. On every occasion the report was that Canadian cattle were perfectly free from the disease with which they had been credited. From that time on I believe every Government in this country has been bringing to the attention of the authorities in England the falseness of that accusation levied against Canadian stock breeders. I would, however, be very sorry if this Parliament went on record as in any way seeking to interfere with the rights and liberties of the Mother Country. We have not only jealously guarded our national status but we have exalted it to such a degree that not long ago Right Hon. Bonar Law announced in the House of Commons that if Canada wished complete independence, there would be no opposition from the Mother Country. How can we, in the face of such statements, interfere with what is a domestic right of the British authorities? I hope the implication that has been levied againsf the stock breeders and the cattle of this country can be removed, but I shall be very sorry to see this Government in order to gain that end go out of its

way to interfere with the affairs of the Mother Country. Canada has placed her case before the British authorities, and having done that she should rest her energies at that point. Further than that, we have no right to go, and I cerainly think we should not go.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has stated that the British authorities no longer take the view that Canadian cattle are diseased, but they say that it is possible for diseased cattle to come from the United States into Canada and in that way get to England. If that be the case, if the British authorities no longer take the position that this embargo was imposed on Canadian cattle because of their being diseased, it seems we are hammering a straw man very hard. But there is one ground on which I think both these resolutions should be withdrawn, and that is, that it is quite evident from the newspapers to-day that the question of embargo or no embargo is an active political question before the British electorate. It certainly has not been stated in the press that one side are saying that Canadian cattle are diseased and the other side saying that they are not diseased. The question that was raised for the British electorate to decide was this: Do you want an embargo or not? If you have no embargo, you are going to have cheaper food in Great Britain. They are not saying: you are going to have diseased cattle. The opposition to that, whatever it was, is not stated, and it is immaterial so long as the other side do not take and have not taken the position that the embargo is imposed because Canadian cattle are diseased. Therefore, there is before the British electorate to-day the issue of cheap food; it is an active political question, and it is not in the interest of the people of Canada or the Canadian Parliament to express any further opinion on this question at this time by a resolution of this House. Let the British people fight out their domestic questions as they like. The British authorities are not slandering us before the people of Great Britain today; we should let them follow their own course in their political matters, and let us attend to a few things we have to do here ourselves.

I think I am in order in speaking to the amendment, and I should like to make a suggestion to the hon. member for South Renfrew

(Mr. Pedlow). I quite agree Hvith the attitude of my hon. friend (Mr. Bristol), and I think the position, which I took myself and which I understood him to support on general grounds, apart, of course, from my incursion into fiscal matters, gained a very strong reinforcement from his drawing attention to the fact that these matters are exciting the attention of the people of Great Britain politically.
I rose, however, for the jpurpose of stating clearly what I understand to be-Britain's position in this matter. I think it is well our people should understand it without any possibility of doubt as to the actual facts of the case. If I am wrong, I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) will correct me, or my hon. friend to whose speech we all listened with the greatest possible interest. Some talk as if Great Britain were doing something specially directed against Canada on this question. The Minister of Agriculture can tell the House far better than I can of the immense value of the British herds of cattle, and how owners of British herds from time to time sell cattle at almost fabulous prices. Having regard to the value of those cattle, the British Government have for years taken the position that they will play doubly safe in regard to the health of their cattle within their shores. That is the position they took to begin with, and they take it still. If they admit, what they have to admit, that we have a very fine bill of health amongst our stock in Canada, they still have a fear about diseased cattle coming in from the United States. They play safe within their borders in regard to the health of their extremely valuable cattle, and they put on this embargo, not specially against Canada, but, as I understand the matter, against all countries in the world. Do they take live cattle in from any country except to kill them at the port of debarkation?
Not without a special license.

Not without a license do they take them from anywhere. I think it is important, with a view towards the best possible relationships and understanding between the Canadian and the British people, that the fact should be known, that this is not a special act against Canada; that it is an act that is undertaken along the line of extreme caution in the preservation of the health of their herds. In view of that fact, I very much doubt the wis-

dom of successive Governments in doing what the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said they are doing, and that is how I view the question. He has said, as I have said before him, that in Canada we should resent very quickly and ferociously any interference with our affairs. There is no text upon which I have heard so many sermons preached in this House as that of Canadian autonomy, and this question is one of British autonomy. On that ground I would appeal to the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow) to think carefully before he presses his amendment, and I appeal to him specially on another ground. We are told that all Governments in Canada have taken a line of action which the Prime Minister tells us this Government is taking. I am sure, if there is anything that would infuse a doubt into the mind of the hon. member for Renfrew South about the wisdom of this course of protest, it would be that it is being undertaken by the present Government. I should like him to think twice before he undertakes to press an amendment before this House to put himself in wrong with the people in specially reinforcing an action of the Government against which he so cheerfully voted a want of all confidence the other day.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would very
gladly vote for the amendment of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow), if it were founded on fact, but I think he is mistaken. He proposes to say that the Government should make a strong protest against the reason that Canadian cattle are diseased being assigned by the government of Great Britain as an excuse for placing the embargo. I do not think the British Government do assign that as a reason. They may have done so in years gone by; I am not going to dispute that, but in all recent discussion of the matter to which I have had my attention drawn, no such reason has been assigned. Quite the contrary. They admit that Canadian cattle are not diseased, and the whole argument now is that unless they have the embargo American cattle may enter Great Britain through Canada. I do not argue whether that is right or wrong, but that is their ground, and if they allege that as a ground we ought not to put on record something else. I would call the attention of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) to that. I think his resolution states as a fact that which we have no evidence of. I
do not think it is a fact. I do not believe he could quote from any recent utterance of the President of the Board of Agriculture or of any other British minister in the recent discussion in the Dudley election, for example, which would warrant the statement that the British Government has used as an excuse the allegation that our cattle are diseased; and if that is not founded in fact, why should we vote for it here?
Is there any official information on record either here or in the Old Country setting forth the facts that the hon. member is now trying to illustrate?

Would it not be in
order for me to ask him if there is anything on record for what he says? We are not bound to prove a negative.
It is common talk on the street and in the press, that disease is the reason for the embargo.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
require such written documents as evidence as some hon. members seem to require. Mr. Bennett, a former member of this House, in his speech before all the Press Delegates in Calgary, gave as a reason why Canadian cattle were prohibited from entering Great Britain-and he called it a slander on the cattle of Canada; I do not know whether he said that the British Government gave this as a reason-that it was on account of disease. That is sufficient evidence for me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon.
gentleman will look at the record of the 1907 conference he will see that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is right. The British Government do not assign disease as a reason. They have abandoned that, but the implication is there because of the cause for which the embargo was originally imposed.

Yes, it is there. They
have sent abroad the statement that they were refusing our cattle because they were diseased, and here we have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) who tells us that that statement is not true. It is a slander on our cattle, and I think we should take some action to show that we resent it. If the embargo is not being maintained for the reason that was assigned in the first place, let the British government come out and say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They have done so.
They have?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think so.

They should do so. If
it was any other country we would protest. I do not think we should allow this stigma to rest on our cattle. It is not fair that one of our staple exports should be allowed to rest under the imputation of being diseased. The impression still prevails; it is common talk in the street, and is discussed in the press. When you travel on the railway trains you will hear everybody asking why the embargo on Canadian cattle is maintained, and the reason given is that the cattle are not fit to be consumed by English people or anybody else. I say that we should take steps to remove this stigma on our cattle, and if this is the best means, I am going to vote for the amendment, I think some of our friends are a little bit too ticklish.
Oh, oh.
Do not laugh. Some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken would have called the hon. member for South Renfrew disloyal-
No, no.

Yes, yes. I have been
through the mill, boys, and I know. We are here to transact business, and I am going to vote in favour of a resolution that will have the effect of making the British Government dispel the idea that our cattle are diseased. They have created that impression, and I think it is only right that

we should say we do not like it, and feel that they should dispel it.

I would suggest, in view of the
statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and of/ the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, (Mr. Fielding) and as it is now ten minutes to six o'clock, that it would be well to let this resolution stand until it can be licked into such shape that everybody could vote for it. So far as I can understand, there appears to be a great difference of opinion about nothing. We do not want to make ourselves ridiculous unnecessarily. I do not claim to know very much about the subject, but I have read in the papers reports of meetings where British ministers have stated that there was no disease among our cattle in Canada, and that they were not afraid of disease being carried to the English herds. I think we should let the resolution stand in the meantime.

In the debate it has been generally
admitted that the herds of Canada are practically free from disease. My hon. friend from Red Deer, when speaking of the splendid reputation for health that British cattle enjoy, apparently forgot that frequently throughout the British Isles there is an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease.
I must correct my hon. friend as to a matter of fact. I said nothing whatever about disease among British cattle; I spoke of their immense money value.

In that regard there is
no difference between their herds and our herds, which are also of immense money value. The people of Great Britain by implication say that our Canadian cattle are diseased. Now it would be just as logical for us in Canada to say that we would not admit British cattle because frequently there are outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease in the herds of Great Britain and their cattle are subject to tubercular trouble. It is a matter of record that any herds coming from the British Isles are quarantined. Sometimes the cattle are returned, and sometimes they are allowed to come in and spread this disease. I think that we in this Parliament, representing the people of Canada, would be just as well justified in putting on an embargo against British cattle on those grounds, as the British Government is justified in maintaining an embargo against our cattle

because sometimes there is disease among our herds. I agree with those who have advanced the argument that we should say to Great Britain: Very well, if you wish to keep our cattle out, you can put on a tariff; but remove this stigma from our herds.

I think we have all listened with very great interest to the debate that has taken place this afternoon, especially as it is a question that is affecting the farmers throughout Ontario to a considerable degree at the present time; not that the farmers themselves perhaps are so deeply interested in it, but the question has been raised in the province of Ontario by the Minister of Agriculture for the province, for reasons which he can perhaps better explain than I can. However, the statement of the mover of the original resolution this afternoon was one worthy of the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith), and one which clearly convinces us still further that he is eminently fitted for the important positions which he has held for many years in the livestock organizations of this province. The reply of the hon. minister was, I am sure, one that appealed to us all as a most businesslike statement.
I do not think I have ever seen any statement on the question which appealed to me more than that made by the minister this afternoon, which put some phases of the matter in a way that must appeal to us very forcibly. The amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) is two-fold, and with both phases of it I heartily agree. One aspect of that amendment is its approval of the course of this Government. The hon. member moves that a protest be entered against the action of the British Government, and this is a policy which has been followed by this Government ever since it came into power, and, in fact, by every Government, I think, which has been in power in Canada since the embargo was imposed. The amendment is therefore, an approval not only of the Government that holds the reins of power to-day, but also of previous Governments. But I also interpret it as a disapproval of the policy which has been adopted by the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario. The amendment to the resolution says that this Parliament, and the Canadian people represented by this Parliament, should make a protest against the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario. That minister says:	"I am going
over to create an agitation in Britain among the people which will be so strong that it will compel the British Government to remove the embargo." Some of his colleagues assert that the embargo is going to be removed as a result of his visit to England; and, further than that, they say that if it is removed he is going to receive all the credit therefor. Leaving that aside for the moment, let us consider what the likely results will be of the action of the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario in going to Britain at this time and taking part in the by-elections there, where this question is being discussed by the people. I think that instead of assisting the farmers of Canada in securing the removal of the embargo, his action will embitter the British people and create a feeling of resentment among them which will not easily subside; and instead of aiding the cause which he professes to have at heart, which this Parliament is anxious to aid, and which the Government has been endeavouring to bring to a successful issue, he is going to create new difficulties for the Government, which will probably have the effect of retarding the removal * of the embargo. It being six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned without question being put pursuant to rule.
Thursday, March 10, 1921
